output.title: Why transcript accuracy is not the real question
output.body:
For a small business owner, the real question is not, “How accurate is the transcript?” It is, “What decision or action does this transcript enable, and who makes it?” That is the practical boundary when you are comparing a bounded automation investment with doing the work manually or hiring someone to do it.

A useful example is customer calls. A transcript only matters if it helps someone act on a refund request, a technical issue, or a follow-up commitment. If the transcript is just stored in a folder, or someone has to read it again by hand, you have improved the text, not the workflow. Neat, but not the point.

The control boundary is human approval. For money movement and other high-risk decisions, a person still has to review before anything irreversible happens. In that setup, “accurate enough” means accurate enough to reach the right reviewer with the right context, not perfect in the abstract.

So the next step is to ask one diagnostic question: what happens to this transcript after it is generated? If the answer is “nothing,” transcript accuracy is not the bottleneck. If the answer is “it feeds a decision or a downstream system,” then accuracy, routing, and human check-in become the workflow to design.

That is usually where the work gets clearer. Not glamorous, but useful.
